en: And the settled land of Talas remained.
The ruined Argyn people remained.
Red gold and abundant goods,
Countless equal treasures remained.
Many lamenting heroes remained.
When his beard was white as a swan,
When his journey drew near,
As he mounted to ride toward death,
When Almighty Allah was to grant
The true abode from which none return—
He seemed somehow different,
With the look of one who would interrogate,
Yet he did not seize the reins
And turn the mouth of the sorrel, hardened by trials.
Saying, “It is the funeral feast of my father, Khan Bakai,”
We did not take charge of the feast;
We did not break open with axes
The countless treasuries and myriad stores.
At Khan Bakai’s funeral feast
We did not scatter riches lavishly.
We did not throng the lower road,
Infidel and Muslim alike,
All crying out, “Khan Bakai!”
We did not honor him with a funeral feast;
Infidel and Muslim alike,
We never gathered everyone together;
For my uncle, sovereign Bakai,
We did not hold a splendid feast.
Under the enemy’s bullets of steel,
In the cruel snare of suffering,
My aged kinsman must be enduring torment
In Kanchoro’s hands.
Suffering much abuse from mighty men,
Weary Bakai must have grown;
His reason fled and senses lost,
Wretched Bakai must have grown.
To the appointed place of death
Bakai must have gone;
Stripped of mane and tail,
Alas, old Bakai
Must have been left hornless,
His horn broken, brought to shame,
He must have been left helpless.
The people did not cry out, the nation did not stir;
For my dear uncle Bakai
They held no honored funeral feast.
The land did not thunder, the people did not clamor;
My forefather, old Bakai,
Saw no such splendid rites.
Though grief must have smoldered and flared,
We cast no handfuls of earth;
We witnessed none of the rites,
And my warrior uncle Bakai
We did not lay in a deep-dug grave,
Saying, “The father of the nation is dead,”
Nor bury him with our own hands.
We did not gather at his hands and feet;
Upon my warrior uncle Bakai
We cast no handful of earth.
For my lionhearted uncle Bakai
We held no fitting funeral feast.
With six fleet-footed horses
And letters broad as a palm,
To all four corners of the world
We did not ride four circuits.
We did not summon the noble peoples
And hold Khan Bakai’s funeral feast.
The streamers of his great banner
We did not cut in motley red;
Saying, “My father Khan Bakai is dead,”
Infidel and Muslim alike,
We did not gather every last one.
At Bakai’s solemn funeral feast,
Infidel and Muslim alike,
With all the people gathered round,
At my father Khan Bakai’s feast,
Their weapons laid ready,
Bare swords belted on,
Matchlocks slung at their waists,
Raging like hungry lions,
The clamoring people fell silent;
Semetey, lofty as a mountain peak,
Slung his white musket over his shoulder.
The match of the white musket,
Flashing in many colors,
To an enemy watching warily
Appeared like a towering mountain.
When he opened his cavernous mouth,
From the gray wolf’s jaws
Blue flame came pouring forth.
He ranged along the Sombuk River,
And slaughtered every man who fought him;
None who faced him remained alive.
Your forebear, your ancestral sire,
Crushed all who crossed him,
And laid waste all he encountered;
He drove mad all who faced him,
And none who traded shots survived.
Such a khan was your father,
And that father’s younger brother
Was the renowned Shygai.
Shygai’s son was Chynkojo,
Who grew arrogant and divided the people,
Stirring the masses and ruining the land.
They bound tassels upon pinewood spears
And made war upon your father.
He fled and joined Toltoi,
Crossing defiles and leading forces over ridges;
The mad wretch died in the blaze of war,
After gathering the people and leading an army,
And raising strife against your father.
They loosed arrows like pouring rain
And fired bullets like hail,
Seeking to unleash chaos
And seize your mother, Khan Akun’s daughter,
From your father.
For ages armies filled the land,
And the bloody turmoil grew immense;
For forty days they fought without rest,
The Jediger and the Kyrgyz facing one another.
A hero favored by the spirits died,
A vigorous warrior in his prime died,
The skillful champion Aizaker died,
And mighty Alymy Toltoi died.
They kept launching mass assaults,
Firing muskets and loosing bows,
And we fought in bloody close combat.
As for Kojo, the son of Shygai,
He began the conflict, and we slew him.
Yesterday we began a glorious slaughter;
Among the champions, valiant Bakai
Must have moved like a wolf in the goat-game.
My heroic mother Kanykei,
Under the cruel khan’s bullets,
Was captured as plunder and made a slave,
Burning to ashes in her anguish,
Like ragged, matted wool.
She became Kanchoro’s slave,
Her back strained and stooped,
Her eyes bulging as she tended calves;
She must have aged before her time.
Unable to escape humiliation,
That poor woman heard no word from us
To tell her we were safe and well.
She could neither cease her sobbing
Nor surrender her soul and die;
Her wits scattered in bewilderment,
A film veiling her darkened eyes,
Quarreling even with dumb beasts,
Her dear face wrinkled,
She must be living in torment.
Blazing in anguish, turned to embers,
Her soul embittered and tightly knotted,
Now dying, now flaring like fire,
This must be what became of her.
“My son Seytek, listen well:
When your poor uncle speaks,
He has suffered countless evils.
His sorrow is a wondrous tale to tell.
From our own kin we suffered humiliation;
From those nearest us we met disgrace,
Affliction, misery, and great hardship.
Yesterday in Kara-Buura and Chatkal,
With your warrior father at their head,
When the Kyrgyz ranged proudly there,
Your ancestral sire was of noble stock,
And every one of your fathers was a khan;
Whoever fought them met his grave.
Your ancient forefather was named Nogoi—
And Nogoi was no easy foe.
Such is this wretched world,”
Said Külchoro, and thus
He finished his sorrowful account,
His heart choked with bitter grief.
The gray-wolf hero mounted his horse,
And from his falconlike, beloved eyes
Tears fell without a blink;
Grief-stricken, he folded his hands
And broke into ringing sobs.
As Külchoro stood weeping,
Old Kyzylsart began to cry,
And all the gathered people cried;
Overcome, the hero Seytek cried,
And all who understood cried,
Weeping that such bleak calamity
Could befall a man.
Then the hero Seytek’s
Eyes blazed like a lion’s;
Angrily he ground his teeth,
Wrathfully preparing himself,
And to the enraged Seytek
Wisdom came from the unseen.
The keen gray wolf grew restless,
And the mature Seytek roused himself:
“May my poor head never flinch;
If I do not choose and mount Taiküröң,
If this year I do not charge the foe unafraid,
If I do not beat the madness
From the hateful enemy’s skull,
If I do not wreak a glorious slaughter,
If I do not avenge this year
My father who passed into eternity,
May I die before I am born,
May I sink away unborn!
If the son of a prince
Cannot shatter the flood and move his people,
Cannot shake the world and take revenge,
Cannot overthrow the chief and spill his blood,
Cannot fight and take lives,
Cannot thrust his spear and break their ranks—
The mighty Toltoi and Chynkojo
We destroyed in carnage.
When we met them in battle
And slew their heroes,
The warrior most skilled with the spear died,
And the mightiest man in all the world died.
Many khans who came were slain,
And everyone we encountered died.
Over branching passes and high slopes
That was the road we used to travel;
Those whom we fought, your uncle
Swept away with his army.
While the great warrior lived,
Your lionhearted uncle was a hero,
A lion and gray wolf of a champion
Who made the whole world submit.
The one who crushed all challengers—
Alas, that Choro was I.
My fortune failed, my strength departed,
The panther, the gray-wolf hero, was gone;
My days passed in servitude,
And now, my son, brave Seytek,
I stand before you ruined thus.
While the panther lived,
I carved up whole fat-tailed sheep to eat.
I used to wonder where hell,
The greatest misery and disaster, could be.
While my magnanimous lord lived,
I knew the world and filled it with uproar;
When I lost my generous lord,
I suffered torment and withered away.
When I rode to battle, I lacked nothing,
And carved up fat-tailed sheep to eat;
While my mighty uncle lived,
I used to say I would wreak slaughter
Not only among the Kyrgyz, but across the world.
There is no strength left in the waist I gird,
My heroic, generous champion is gone;
What lives today is gone tomorrow.
One day all will be crushed—
Yet you lie there voicing your regrets.
When you took aim
At an enemy who defied you,
Compelling the whole world to submit,
When you held dominion over it,
Breaking through dead ends and opening roads,
